name: OptLogger (block string copy in lock-free async logger)
listed_description: Variant of the book's asynchronous queue-based logger that copies char* arguments into a fixed-size string log element in one block instead of pushing one character at a time.
claim_text: Average 25757 clock cycles per log() call for original logger versus 466 for optimized, roughly 50 times faster.
book_benchmark: logger_benchmark (Chapter12/benchmarks/logger_benchmark.cpp): 100,000 log() calls each with a random 128-character string, RDTSC cycles averaged per call, original Common::Logger versus OptCommon::OptLogger, release CMake build on a four-core ThinkPad X1 Carbon laptop at about 2.6 GHz; compiler and flags not stated here, single run.
guessed_baseline: same book's per-character Logger::pushValue(const char*) implementation (not a third-party logger)
found_in: book: Building Low Latency Applications with C++ (2023), ch. 12, Benchmarking Logger string optimization

name: OptMemPool (assert-free release build object pool)
listed_description: Variant of the book's fixed-capacity memory pool where ASSERT checks in allocate() and deallocate() compile out when NDEBUG is defined.
claim_text: Original MemPool 343 clock cycles per operation versus 44 for OptMemPool, a speedup of around 7 to 8 times.
book_benchmark: release_benchmark (Chapter12/benchmarks/release_benchmark.cpp): allocate 256 MDPMarketUpdate objects then deallocate them, repeated 100,000 times, RDTSC cycles per allocate/deallocate call, MemPool versus OptMemPool, release build on the four-core ThinkPad laptop at about 2.6 GHz; single run, compiler and flags not stated here.
guessed_baseline: same book's MemPool with assertions enabled (not malloc or a third-party pool)
found_in: book: Building Low Latency Applications with C++ (2023), ch. 12, Benchmarking release build optimization

name: std::array direct-indexed hash maps in limit order book (MEOrderBook)
listed_description: Order book that stores orders and price levels in fixed-size std::array tables indexed directly by client id, order id and price, compared with the same book using std::unordered_map.
claim_text: Array hash map 142650 clock cycles per operation versus 152457 for std::unordered_map, about 6 to 7% overhead for unordered_map.
book_benchmark: hash_benchmark (Chapter12/benchmarks/hash_benchmark.cpp): 100,000 generated NEW and CANCEL requests applied to MEOrderBook (array-based) versus UnorderedMapMEOrderBook, RDTSC cycles averaged per add()/cancel() call, release build on the four-core ThinkPad laptop at about 2.6 GHz; single run, results vary between runs.
found_in: book: Building Low Latency Applications with C++ (2023), ch. 12, Growing and enhancing the hash maps

name: RDTSC cycle counter timing macros (START_MEASURE / END_MEASURE)
listed_description: Inline-assembly rdtsc wrapper and macros for cheap in-code latency measurement, used instead of wall-clock calls.
claim_text: rdtsc() is significantly faster than std::chrono::system_clock::now() or clock_gettime(); no numbers given.
book_benchmark: No timing of rdtsc against clock_gettime or chrono in this chunk; qualitative claim only. Code is Chapter11/common/perf_utils.h.
found_in: book: Building Low Latency Applications with C++ (2023), ch. 11, Adding overhead due to instrumentation

name: Templates and CRTP in place of std::function callbacks
listed_description: Book proposes replacing std::function callbacks in sockets, TCP server and trade engine with compile-time polymorphism (templates, CRTP); left as an exercise, not implemented here.
claim_text: Calls through std::function are slower than direct calls and incur costs similar to virtual functions; no numbers given.
book_benchmark: None; no benchmark or code for this change in the chunk.
found_in: book: Building Low Latency Applications with C++ (2023), ch. 12, Eliminating the use of std::function instances

name: Boost.Unordered (boost::unordered_flat_map and related)
